# Image-generation capability: discovery result

**No callable image generator is available in this session.** Recorded here as the
protocol requires, together with what was done instead. The gate is **not** skipped —
real, viewable mockups are in `design/` and `design-directions.json`.

## What was probed

| Capability | Result |
|---|---|
| MCP servers | `.mcp.json` declares `{}` — none configured |
| Host tools (incl. deferred/lazy-loaded) | Searched for image generation/editing; none exists. Available deferred tools are cron, worktree, DesignSync, RemoteTrigger, WebFetch/WebSearch, etc. |
| Generation API credentials | No `OPENAI_*`, `ANTHROPIC_*`, `GEMINI_*`, `REPLICATE_*`, `STABILITY_*`, `FAL_*` or similar keys in the environment |
| Local generative tooling | `ffmpeg` present; no Stable Diffusion / ComfyUI / Blender / `magick` |

## Stock photography sourcing was also constrained

- `api.pexels.com` → **401** (key required, none supplied).
- `unsplash.com` search (site and `napi`) → **401 bot challenge** (Anubis), both via `curl` and a real Chromium session.
- `pexels.com` rendered search via Playwright → works, but **rate-limits after ~2 queries per session**. Two queries succeeded; the following eleven returned nothing across three attempts each.
- `api.openverse.org` → works, but returns incoherent, mostly `by-nc-nd` material unusable as a coherent nine-garment set.

A contact sheet of the Pexels results was inspected (`design/contact.png`): mixed subject,
mixed light, several irrelevant. Not a coherent product set for a fictional label.

## Substitution used, per the skill's named fallback

`VISUAL_DESIGN.md`: *"If generation is unavailable, use supplied images or a
material-backed visual composition in a capable design tool/browser, and name the substitution."*

Both directions were therefore **authored as real page compositions in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas and
rendered to PNG through headless Chromium at 1440px and 390px**. These are actual rendered
images of actual designs, not prompts and not sourced references relabelled as mockups.

The garment imagery is likewise **authored**: nine drawn technical "flats"
(`design/flats.mjs`, inspected at plate scale in `design/flats.png`), one consistent
drawing system, one shared scale. This satisfies the brief's requirement for coherent,
representative clothing imagery that never implies a verified photograph of fictional
inventory — both directions label it as such on the page.

The three photographs that did survive sourcing (Pexels, free licence) appear in
direction B only, as halftoned atmosphere, never as a product view.

**Consequence for phase two:** without a generator, product views stay drawn rather than
photographic. If the reviewer can supply photography or a generation route, direction B
absorbs it with no structural change (it already mixes drawn plates with halftoned photography);
direction A would need a full nine-garment photographic set to change medium.

import fs from 'node:fs'

const A = `THE UNROLL — a cinematic scrub on a dark ink field, where one column of cloth runs the whole page.

THE IDEA
The page behaves like a single length of cloth being unrolled past a camera that never cuts. A tall
"cloth column" appears in the hero holding plate 01 (Chore Jacket) and it is the same element, unbroken,
that later splits into the product grid. Continuity is literal: one object owned by one animation, carried
from lookbook into shop. Ink #0F1216, ecru cloth #DED6C6, one vermilion #C5462C used only for state
(current size, add-to-bag, free-delivery progress, scrub head). Type is Archivo with its width axis pushed
to 125% for the display, giving a 132px hero lockup that is uppercase, tight and industrial, over an
ordinary 15px UI face — high contrast between voice and instrument.

PRIMARY JOURNEY
Hero ("ONE PRICE / ALL YEAR", the real one-line brand statement, plate 01 in the column) →
The Unroll, a pinned stage that scrub-scrubs through nine authored crops, entry / hold on construction /
release, captioned with each garment's real fabric statement and price →
The Handoff, where the last frame's column splits into three and keeps its cloth →
The Shop: sticky filter rail with live counts and the "Showing N of 9" line, a three-up grid of cards each
carrying name, category, price, detail, fabric, colours, five size chips with sold-out struck through, and
Add to bag → an inline bag with named lines, per-line Remove, subtotal, free-delivery progress and total →
Sizing (full five-row chart plus an annotated flat and the between-sizes advice) → Care as four numbered
statements → Shipping & returns, all three regions plus 60 days and same-day exchange → three reviews →
colophon carrying the eleven-people, four-factories and no-sales facts.

IMAGERY
Nine drawn technical flats, already built and inspected (design/flats.mjs, design/flats.png): one line
system, one shared scale so a shirt genuinely reads shorter than a trouser. Rendered in the "ink" palette
for this direction. No photography at all — the direction is deliberately graphic, which is what makes the
absence of a photo studio a choice rather than a shortfall. A standing line states the images are drawn
illustrations, not photographs of stock. Fonts: Archivo (variable width) from Google Fonts, self-hosted.
Nothing else needs sourcing.

MOTION (the real mechanism)
One scroll-driven timeline over a position:sticky stage, no scroll hijack, native scrolling preserved.
A single owner writes transform/clip-path on the column element; scroll progress maps to an authored
keyframe list of crops (scale + translate + which garment is visible), so pushing in on the corozo buttons
and pulling back out is authored framing, not a generic zoom. The handoff is a FLIP: at the end of the
pinned range the column's measured rect is interpolated into the first three card rects, so the identical
node lands in the grid — reversible, resize-safe, interrupt-safe. Parallax is limited to the type rail
drifting against the column at a different rate. No video, no pixelation: this direction spends its whole
motion budget on one continuous camera.

MOBILE (390px)
Hero stacks: type first at 62px, the column below as a 440px full-bleed band. The pinned stage keeps its
pin but shortens to one frame at a time with a visible progress rail, and is swipe-scrubbable as well as
scroll-driven. Filters become a horizontally scrolling rail; the grid drops to one column; size chips grow
to flex:1 so every target clears 44px; the bag becomes a bottom sheet. See design/a-4-mobile.png and
design/a-5-mobile-shop.png — the reflow is real, already rendered at 390px.

REDUCED MOTION
The stage un-pins entirely and becomes a stacked sequence of the same nine framed crops with their captions;
the handoff becomes an immediate cut to the grid. Nothing is hidden and no content depends on animation.

IMPLEMENTATION
React + Vite, plain CSS, no runtime dependency added. One IntersectionObserver + scroll handler feeding a
rAF loop writing to CSS custom properties; CSS grid everywhere else. Filter, size selection and bag stay
ordinary React state on the existing App.jsx logic. The prototype slice to build first is the pinned stage's
last frame through the FLIP into card 01 — entry, development and exit — at both widths, because that join
is the only genuinely uncertain part.

UNCERTAINTY
The FLIP across a sticky-to-static boundary is the risk: getting the release point to resolve to the current
layout under fast reversal and under resize. Mitigated by measuring on every run rather than caching
coordinates. Second risk: a 132px display lockup and a 9-frame pinned stage is a long runway before the
first product — the scrub range must stay short enough that a shopper who just wants the jacket is not
trapped. A persistent "Skip to shop" in the bar handles that.

COST
Higher. The flats exist; the expense is the pinned-scrub timeline and the FLIP, plus testing reversal,
interruption and resize. Roughly two-thirds of the build budget lands on one mechanism.`

const B = `PLATE & PRESS — a printed catalogue on paper, where every photograph prints itself in halftone as you reach it.

THE IDEA
The shop is a printed object. Warm paper #EFE9DD, ink #16150F, one press red #B3301C for registration and
state. Instrument Serif at 62px for the voice, Roboto Mono at 10.5px for every technical caption, Newsreader
for reading text — the split between "editorial" and "specification" is the whole typographic system.
The nine garments are nine numbered plates (I–IX) on a contact sheet. The focal device is a real halftone:
photographs are re-printed as ink dots on paper by a canvas routine, and the dot cell shrinks from coarse to
fine as the image crosses the fold — the picture literally prints itself as you arrive. This is already
working and rendered, not described: see the three states in design/b-1-opening.png.

PRIMARY JOURNEY
Masthead ("Catalogue eleven — Leeds — no sales, ever") → frontispiece spread: a serif statement beside a
full-height halftoned photograph, with a real index of all nine plates (roman numeral, name, category,
price, dotted leaders) that doubles as the fastest route to any garment → The Device band, three states of
one plate resolving → The Sheet: a registration bar carrying the filter with live counts and the
"Showing N of 9" line, then a 3×3 ruled contact sheet where each plate carries name, category, price,
detail, fabric, colours, a single joined five-cell size selector with sold-out cells hatched, and the
add button → the opened plate: the chosen plate lifted off the sheet and enlarged beside the bag, which
names each line's garment, size and price with per-line Remove, subtotal, free-delivery progress and total →
spec sheet (annotated flat + the full five-row chart + between-sizes advice) → Care set as marginalia, mono
notes in the left margin against large serif statements → Shipping & returns, all three regions, 60 days,
same-day exchange → three reviews as pull quotes → colophon carrying the three shop facts.

IMAGERY
Two media, kept strictly apart. Product views are the same nine drawn flats (paper palette) — they are the
only thing you buy from, and they are labelled as drawn illustrations. Atmosphere is real photography,
sourced free-licence from Pexels (cotton detail, folded cloth, a making shot), used only halftoned and
captioned "Representative image · not stock". Because halftone flattens exposure and colour, it unifies
photographs that do not otherwise belong together — which is exactly the constraint this session is under,
and the reason this direction is robust to it. Fonts: Instrument Serif, Roboto Mono, Newsreader.

MOTION (the real mechanism)
Halftone resolve: an offscreen canvas samples each photograph, auto-levels it, and prints it back as ink
dots; scroll progress across the element drives the dot cell from ~22px to ~3px. One owner, one canvas,
redrawn on a rAF tick with a work cap, at device-pixel-capped size. Filtering is a registration shift: the
sheet does not fade, it re-registers — surviving plates FLIP to their new cells with a short red rule sliding
under the active filter. Selecting a plate lifts it off the sheet and enlarges it into the opened-plate
region, same node, so the garment you chose is the garment you see. Parallax is absent by design; the paper
does not float.

MOBILE (390px)
Masthead stacks, the index stays full-width and stays the fast route. Frontispiece becomes a full-bleed
halftone below the statement, at a coarser minimum cell so the dots stay legible small. The sheet becomes
one plate per row with its rules retained; the size selector spans full width so each cell is a 60px+ target;
the registration bar scrolls horizontally; the opened plate stacks above the bag. Rendered at 390px in
design/b-4-mobile.png and design/b-5-mobile-sheet.png.

REDUCED MOTION
Every canvas renders once at its finest cell — the photograph, printed, immediately. Filtering cuts rather
than re-registers; the plate opens without the lift. The halftone stays, because it is the art direction,
not the animation.

IMPLEMENTATION
React + Vite, plain CSS, no runtime dependency. The halftone is ~40 lines of canvas already written and
proven in design/b.mjs and reusable verbatim. Filter, size selection and bag remain ordinary React state on
the existing App.jsx logic. The prototype slice to build first is one plate resolving from coarse to fine on
real scroll and then FLIPping into the opened-plate view — entry, development and exit — at both widths.

UNCERTAINTY
Canvas cost: several halftone canvases resolving at once on a mid-range phone. Mitigated by only animating
canvases intersecting the viewport, capping backing-store size, and quantising the cell to a small set of
steps so most frames are cache hits. Second risk: at very small cells the dot pattern approaches the source
photo and the device stops reading as a device — the floor stays at ~3px so it always looks printed.

COST
Lower and more predictable than A. The halftone and the sheet both already exist in working form; the
remaining work is wiring scroll progress and the plate FLIP.

this project's actual constraints. Its focal device is already built and inspected rather than promised; its
continuity (plate lifts off the sheet, sheet re-registers under the filter) sits *inside* the shopping task
instead of in front of it, so the brief's "memorable and coherent beyond the hero" and "easy to buy from"
stop competing; and its imagery strategy is the only one that can absorb photography later without a
redesign, since it already mixes drawn plates with halftoned photographs. A's pinned nine-frame scrub is the
more spectacular opening, but it puts its whole budget into a runway before the first garment, and its FLIP
across a sticky boundary is the single riskiest thing in either plan. Choose A if the lookbook spectacle
matters more than the sheet; otherwise B.`

# Photographic assets

Four photographs, all from Pexels under the Pexels License (free to use, no
attribution required; credited here as good practice).

| File | Source | Used as |
|---|---|---|
| `cotton-collar.jpg` | pexels.com/photo/13915356 | Frontispiece plate |
| `cloth-folded.jpg` | pexels.com/photo/4440571 | Device band, plate 1 |
| `tee-folded.jpg` | pexels.com/photo/5746100 | Device band, plate 2 |
| `hung-cotton.jpg` | pexels.com/photo/8532616 | Device band, plate 3 |

These are **representative images of cloth and making**. They are not photographs
of Marlow & Vale inventory, and the page says so — each is captioned
"Representative image · not stock", and the footer repeats it. None of them is
ever used as a product view.

The product views are the drawn technical illustrations in `../flats.js`.
